Am I aware? I... gosh, I don't really know. I'm not sure how to even answer that, to be honest. Because, you know, normally when you're out there on the line, you have to be hyper-aware of literally every single thing. You've got the diesel engines from the excavators rumbling, you've got the walkie-talkie crackling on your shoulder, you've got people commuting who are angry that they're delayed, and you have to watch their tires, watch their eye contact, watch the wind direction so dust doesn't blow in your face... it's a very sensory-heavy environment. You have to be dialed in. 

So normally, I'm taking all of that in. But when that... that heavy wall comes down, and my mind just completely empties out? I really couldn't tell you if I'm hearing the walkie-talkie or not. I mean, my eyes are open. I'm still standing there on my feet, holding the paddle, so my body obviously knows it's standing upright on the pavement, but as for my brain... I just don't know if I'm actually registering any of the input. 

I've tried to think back afterward, you know, after my brain sort of reboots and the thoughts finally start moving again. I try to piece together if I actually saw that white Ford F-150 drive past or if it was already gone by the time I snapped out of it, but I just can't tell. It's almost like asking someone if they remember what was happening in the room while they were asleep. You know you were physically there, your eyes might even be open staring right at the gravel, but you can't really vouch for what was going on around you. So, yeah, I've tried to pay attention to whether I'm taking things in during those moments, but I honestly just don't know if I'm aware of what's happening or not. I haven't been able to figure that part out.

Like a switch flipping? Yes. Exactly like that. It's not a gradual fade-out at all, it's... well, honestly, that suddenness is the whole reason I finally made the appointment to come in here and see you in the first place. I came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times, and it happens so fast that I can't even brace myself for it.

The switch flips. And suddenly, I cannot remember the steps I have done for years. 

I'll be staring at the paddle, this simple piece of equipment I've held for thousands of hours, and in that split second, all the procedures are just gone. I don't know what I'm supposed to do with it. Or I'll look at the paperwork, and I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I'm an educated woman, but suddenly the boxes on the form mean absolutely nothing to me. I completely forget the standard procedure for logging the lane closure. 

If it came on gradually, you know, maybe I could radio the foreman and say, "Hey, I need to step off the asphalt for a minute, I need someone to cover my spot." I could prepare for it, I could keep myself and the crew safe. But because it just hits me out of nowhere, right in the middle of a task I've done a million times... it's just completely unmanageable. I can't keep standing out there having my brain just instantly delete my knowledge of how to do my job. So, yes, it's very sudden. Just completely all at once.

Like someone just walked over and pulled the plug on a television set. \n\nI'll be standing there on the shoulder of the road, and maybe I was just thinking about the traffic flow, or listening to the radio chatter from the pilot car, or even just thinking about what I packed for lunch, and then suddenly... just dead air. Nothing. I don't feel panicked because I don't feel *anything*. There aren't any thoughts there to even be afraid with, if that makes sense? It's just this heavy, thick emptiness. And I'll just stand there, staring at the asphalt or the gravel, and it's almost like everything is just on pause. \n\nThe fear really only creeps in *after*, when the thoughts finally start trickling back and I realize, \"Oh my god, I just lost track of what I was doing and a dump truck just blew past my zone.\" But during the actual blank spell? No, no panic. Just... just a total system freeze. Like a computer when the screen locks up and you can't even move the mouse. You just have to sit there and wait for it to reboot. It's just so bizarre, because you'd think I'd be screaming inside, but there's just nothing there to make a sound with.\n\nDoctor: During these blank spells, are you aware of what’s happening around you?\n\nPatient: Am I aware? I... gosh, I don't really know. I'm not sure how to even answer that, to be honest. Because, you know, normally when you're out there on the line, you have to be hyper-aware of literally every single thing. You've got the diesel engines from the excavators rumbling, you've got the walkie-talkie crackling on your shoulder, you've got people commuting who are angry that they're delayed, and you have to watch their tires, watch their eye contact, watch the wind direction so dust doesn't blow in your face... it's a very sensory-heavy environment. You have to be dialed in. \n\nSo normally, I'm taking all of that in. But when that... that heavy wall comes down, and my mind just completely empties out? I really couldn't tell you if I'm hearing the walkie-talkie or not. I mean, my eyes are open. I'm still standing there on my feet, holding the paddle, so my body obviously knows it's standing upright on the pavement, but as for my brain... I just don't know if I'm actually registering any of the input. \n\nI've tried to think back afterward, you know, after my brain sort of reboots and the thoughts finally start moving again. I try to piece together if I actually saw that white Ford F-150 drive past or if it was already gone by the time I snapped out of it, but I just can't tell. It's almost like asking someone if they remember what was happening in the room while they were asleep. You know you were physically there, your eyes might even be open staring right at the gravel, but you can't really vouch for what was going on around you. So, yeah, I've tried to pay attention to whether I'm taking things in during those moments, but I honestly just don't know if I'm aware of what's happening or not. I haven't been able to figure that part out.\n\nDoctor: After one of these blank spells ends, do you ever realize there’s a period of time you can’t account for?\n\nPatient: Missing time? Like, a period I can't account for? No, no, it's really not like that. I mean, it's not like a blackout where I suddenly look at my watch and realize three hours have just vanished into thin air. I know some people describe things like that, where they lose a whole afternoon, but for me it's... well, it's much more contained, I guess you could say. \n\nWhen the thoughts finally start trickling back in and the spell kind of breaks, I'll usually glance right down at my watch—I always wear this cheap, digital waterproof watch because you never know what the weather is going to do out on the site, between the mud and the sudden downpours—and I'll see that it's really only been a few seconds. Maybe a minute, tops. It feels like this massive, heavy, eternal void while I'm actually stuck in it, but the actual clock time hasn't really moved much at all. I'll still be standing in the exact same spot on the asphalt, my boots haven't moved an inch, I'm still holding the paddle exactly how I was, and the same line of traffic is usually still right there, maybe just one or two cars further along in the queue. \n\nSo I'm not losing big chunks of my day. I can account for the time, it's just that the time itself was spent completely empty. It's just a tiny little blip on the clock, even though inside my head it felt like the whole world hit pause. It's really just those specific, empty seconds where my brain was completely frozen.\n\nDoctor: Do these blank spells start all at once, like a switch flipping, or do they come on gradually?\n\nPatient: Like a switch flipping? Confused? Oh, absolutely. It's... well, it's like waking up from a deep, dreamless sleep, except you're standing upright in the middle of a live construction zone with cars flying by at fifty miles an hour. It takes a minute for the world to sort of... click back into place.

A head injury? Um... no. No, nothing like that at all. I mean, I completely understand why you would ask that, it's a very logical question given what I do for a living. I mean, I know what panic is, like when your heart is pounding out of your chest and you feel like you can't breathe, but it's really not like that at all. \n\nWhen I said it was terrifying before, I meant the *consequences* are terrifying, you know, the reality of the situation with the cars and the heavy machinery and everything. Like someone just walked over and pulled the plug on a television set. \n\nI'll be standing there on the shoulder of the road, and maybe I was just thinking about the traffic flow, or listening to the radio chatter from the pilot car, or even just thinking about what I packed for lunch, and then suddenly... just dead air. Nothing. I don't feel panicked because I don't feel *anything*. There aren't any thoughts there to even be afraid with, if that makes sense? It's just this heavy, thick emptiness. And I'll just stand there, staring at the asphalt or the gravel, and it's almost like everything is just on pause. \n\nThe fear really only creeps in *after*, when the thoughts finally start trickling back and I realize, \"Oh my god, I just lost track of what I was doing and a dump truck just blew past my zone.\" But during the actual blank spell? No, no panic. Just... just a total system freeze. Like a computer when the screen locks up and you can't even move the mouse. You just have to sit there and wait for it to reboot. It's just so bizarre, because you'd think I'd be screaming inside, but there's just nothing there to make a sound with.\n\nDoctor: During these blank spells, are you aware of what’s happening around you?\n\nPatient: Am I aware? I... gosh, I don't really know. I'm not sure how to even answer that, to be honest. Because, you know, normally when you're out there on the line, you have to be hyper-aware of literally every single thing. You've got the diesel engines from the excavators rumbling, you've got the walkie-talkie crackling on your shoulder, you've got people commuting who are angry that they're delayed, and you have to watch their tires, watch their eye contact, watch the wind direction so dust doesn't blow in your face... it's a very sensory-heavy environment. You have to be dialed in. \n\nSo normally, I'm taking all of that in. But when that... that heavy wall comes down, and my mind just completely empties out? I really couldn't tell you if I'm hearing the walkie-talkie or not. I mean, my eyes are open. I'm still standing there on my feet, holding the paddle, so my body obviously knows it's standing upright on the pavement, but as for my brain... I just don't know if I'm actually registering any of the input. \n\nI've tried to think back afterward, you know, after my brain sort of reboots and the thoughts finally start moving again. I try to piece together if I actually saw that white Ford F-150 drive past or if it was already gone by the time I snapped out of it, but I just can't tell. It's almost like asking someone if they remember what was happening in the room while they were asleep. You know you were physically there, your eyes might even be open staring right at the gravel, but you can't really vouch for what was going on around you. So, yeah, I've tried to pay attention to whether I'm taking things in during those moments, but I honestly just don't know if I'm aware of what's happening or not. I haven't been able to figure that part out.\n\nDoctor: After one of these blank spells ends, do you ever realize there’s a period of time you can’t account for?\n\nPatient: Missing time? Like, a period I can't account for? No, no, it's really not like that. I mean, it's not like a blackout where I suddenly look at my watch and realize three hours have just vanished into thin air. I know some people describe things like that, where they lose a whole afternoon, but for me it's... well, it's much more contained, I guess you could say. \n\nWhen the thoughts finally start trickling back in and the spell kind of breaks, I'll usually glance right down at my watch—I always wear this cheap, digital waterproof watch because you never know what the weather is going to do out on the site, between the mud and the sudden downpours—and I'll see that it's really only been a few seconds. Maybe a minute, tops. It feels like this massive, heavy, eternal void while I'm actually stuck in it, but the actual clock time hasn't really moved much at all. I'll still be standing in the exact same spot on the asphalt, my boots haven't moved an inch, I'm still holding the paddle exactly how I was, and the same line of traffic is usually still right there, maybe just one or two cars further along in the queue. \n\nSo I'm not losing big chunks of my day. I can account for the time, it's just that the time itself was spent completely empty. The foreman might get on the radio and tell me to flip my sign for the southbound lane, and I'll realize I just had one of those completely blank moments, but I haven't missed the whole morning. It's just a tiny little blip on the clock, even though inside my head it felt like the whole world hit pause. So, no, I don't really have missing time that I can't account for, not in the sense of looking up at the sun and realizing it's suddenly late afternoon when it was just morning a second ago. It's really just those specific, empty seconds where my brain was completely frozen.\n\nDoctor: Do these blank spells start all at once, like a switch flipping, or do they come on gradually?\n\nPatient: Like a switch flipping? Yes. Exactly like that. It's not a gradual fade-out at all, it's... well, honestly, that suddenness is the whole reason I finally made the appointment to come in here and see you in the first place. I came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times, and it happens so fast that I can't even brace myself for it. \n\nThere's no warning, no feeling of getting foggy or tired first. I will literally be looking right at the daily road-closure forms on my clipboard—the exact same standard forms I've filled out for the county every single morning for years—or I'll be standing out on the line holding the stop-slow paddle, and then, snap. The switch flips. And suddenly, I cannot remember the steps I have done for years. \n\nI'll be staring at the paddle, this simple piece of equipment I've held for thousands of hours, and in that split second, all the procedures are just gone. I don't know what I'm supposed to do with it. Or I'll look at the paperwork, and I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I'm an educated woman, but suddenly the boxes on the form mean absolutely nothing to me. I completely forget the standard procedure for logging the lane closure. \n\nIf it came on gradually, you know, maybe I could radio the foreman and say, \"Hey, I need to step off the asphalt for a minute, I need someone to cover my spot.\" I could prepare for it, I could keep myself and the crew safe. But because it just hits me out of nowhere, right in the middle of a task I've done a million times... it's just completely unmanageable. I can't keep standing out there having my brain just instantly delete my knowledge of how to do my job. So, yes, it's very sudden. Just completely all at once.\n\nDoctor: During one of these blank spells, if someone speaks to you or gives you an instruction, are you able to respond right away?\n\nPatient: Respond right away? Oh, gosh, no. No, not at all. I mean, if someone talks to me while I'm in one of those voids... it's like they're speaking a completely foreign language. Or not even a language, just... noise. \n\nLike I was just telling you a second ago, about how I came in because my mind keeps going completely blank at the absolute worst times? That's exactly how it plays out with other people. If the foreman—say it's Dave, he's usually the one on the main channel—if Dave radios in and says, \"Hey, switch to slow, we've got a cement truck pulling out,\" I might physically hear the static and his voice, but I absolutely cannot respond. Because, like I said, I'll be looking right at that stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. \n\nHow can I respond to an instruction to turn the sign when I don't even remember what the sign is for in that split second? I just stand there. My mouth won't open. I can't tell my hand to move. Or if a commuter rolls down their window—and you know how people get in construction zones, they're so impatient, they lean out and yell, \"Hey lady, how long is this delay going to take?!\"—and I just stare at them. I can't formulate an answer. I can't even process that they're asking me a question about the road closure, because, just like with those forms I mentioned, all my knowledge of the standard procedure is just... wiped. It's temporarily deleted from my brain. \n\nSo, no, I can't respond right away. I can't follow an instruction, I can't answer a question, I can't even say \"hold on a second.\" It takes me however long the blank spell lasts, plus another few seconds of pure, unadulterated panic as my brain tries to reboot and I try to piece together what on earth someone just asked me to do. It's incredibly dangerous, honestly. You can't just have a flagger who can't answer the radio when heavy machinery is moving. It's terrifying, which is exactly why I knew I had to come see you.\n\nDoctor: Outside of these blank spells, have you been having trouble with your memory in everyday life?\n\nPatient: Everyday life? Like, outside of those specific moments when my brain freezes? Um... no, honestly, no. My memory is actually really sharp otherwise. I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I've always been good at retaining information. I don't lose my keys, I remember my grocery lists without having to write them down, I know exactly what time I'm supposed to be at the site every morning, I remember all the guys' names on the crew, their kids' names... so it's not like a general fuzziness or anything like that. I'm not walking into the kitchen and forgetting why I went in there, you know, like people joke about when they hit their forties. \n\nBut, well, like I was trying to explain just a minute ago, that sharp contrast is exactly why this whole thing is so terrifying for me. Because my memory is normally so reliable, it makes it that much more jarring when it just vanishes on me out of nowhere. Like I said, the whole reason I came in is because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. It's not a normal, everyday forgetfulness where I just misplaced a thought. It's that I will look right at the road-closure forms on my clipboard, or I'll be holding that stop-slow paddle out on the asphalt, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. \n\nWhen I'm not in one of those spells, I know those steps backward and forward. I know the exact county protocol for logging a two-lane highway closure versus a four-way intersection. I could do it in my sleep. But then the spell hits, and that specific memory, that deeply ingrained procedural knowledge, is just... inaccessible. It's locked away. So, no, my everyday memory at home or at the grocery store is perfectly fine. It's really just these horrible, specific moments where my mind goes totally blank on the very things I've done a million times.\n\nDoctor: After one of these blank spells ends, do you feel confused for a while afterward?\n\nPatient: Confused? Oh, absolutely. It's... well, it's like waking up from a deep, dreamless sleep, except you're standing upright in the middle of a live construction zone with cars flying by at fifty miles an hour. It takes a minute for the world to sort of... click back into place. \n\nI know I keep hammering on this exact same point, but I just can't stress enough that this is truly the whole reason I came in to see you—because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. And when that switch finally flips back on and the blankness lifts, I don't just instantly go back to normal. I'm left standing there, staring down at those road-closure forms on my clipboard, or gripping the handle of the stop-slow paddle, and the realization washes over me that I just spent the last thirty seconds or whatever completely unable to remember the steps I have done for years. \n\nThat realization brings this massive, suffocating wave of confusion. Did I accidentally wave commuter traffic through into a one-lane choke point? I have to completely re-orient myself to my surroundings. It's this thick, heavy fog of confusion where I'm desperately trying to remember what I was doing right before the void hit, and trying to figure out if I messed anything up while I was gone. \n\nSo it's not just the blank spell itself that's the problem, it's the aftermath, you know? The recovery time. It takes me a good five or ten minutes of just pure, frantic double-checking of my paperwork and the traffic flow to feel like I'm actually grounded in reality again and capable of doing my job safely. It's exhausting, having to constantly rebuild my awareness of what's going on around me. So, yes, the confusion afterward is just... it's profound. It really is.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any head injury around the time these blank spells started?\n\nPatient: A head injury? Um... no. No, nothing like that at all. A headache? You know, I've really tried to pay attention to how my body feels after these episodes, because like I said, the aftermath is just so intense and overwhelming. But a headache? No, I wouldn't say I get a headache. 

I mean, my head feels... full, I guess? But not in a painful way. It's more of that thick, heavy fog I was talking about earlier. It's like my brain is just exhausted from having to reboot itself. Sometimes my neck gets a little stiff, but I think that's just because I tense up so much when the panic sets in. You know, when I realize I've lost time again and I'm frantically looking around at the traffic and the construction equipment, my shoulders just migrate right up to my ears. I'm gripping that stop-slow paddle so tight my knuckles turn white. So any tension I feel up there is definitely just from the sheer stress of the situation, not an actual headache from the spell itself.

It's actually kind of surprising, now that I think about it. You'd think with how jarring it is to have your consciousness just blip out like that, your brain would hurt afterward. Like a computer overheating or something. But no, no throbbing, no sharp pains, no migraines. Just the confusion and the terror and that awful, sinking feeling that I'm losing my grip on things. 

I do get headaches sometimes, obviously, just from being out in the sun all day, the glare off the asphalt, the exhaust fumes from the diesel trucks... it's a harsh environment. But those are totally separate. They don't happen right after the blank spells. The blank spells just leave me feeling completely drained and terrified, but physically, my head doesn't hurt. It's just the mental toll that's so heavy.

I can't keep standing out there having my brain just instantly delete my knowledge of how to do my job. So, yes, it's very sudden. Just completely all at once.\n\nDoctor: During one of these blank spells, if someone speaks to you or gives you an instruction, are you able to respond right away?\n\nPatient: Respond right away? I can't formulate an answer. I can't even process that they're asking me a question about the road closure, because, just like with those forms I mentioned, all my knowledge of the standard procedure is just... wiped. It's temporarily deleted from my brain. \n\nSo, no, I can't respond right away. I can't follow an instruction, I can't answer a question, I can't even say \"hold on a second.\" It takes me however long the blank spell lasts, plus another few seconds of pure, unadulterated panic as my brain tries to reboot and I try to piece together what on earth someone just asked me to do. It's exhausting, having to constantly rebuild my awareness of what's going on around me. So, yes, the confusion afterward is just... it's profound. People get clipped by side mirrors, or a piece of gravel kicks up from a tire, or someone trips over a traffic drum... it's a highly hazardous environment. We have safety briefings every single morning at the site just to drill in how easy it is to get hurt out there. \n\nBut me? No, I haven't had any accidents. I haven't fallen, I haven't bumped my head on the side of the pilot car or any of the heavy machinery. Because then at least there would be a physical explanation for all of this, you know? It would make sense. I could point to a bruise or a concussion and say, \"Okay, that's why my brain is glitching.\" But there was no accident. Nothing physically happened to me to trigger this. \n\nIt just... started. Out of nowhere. Which is why I keep coming back to the fact that my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times, because there is no warning and no physical reason for it. I'll just be standing there on the asphalt, totally unharmed, no head trauma whatsoever, looking right at my clipboard or my stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years. It's just terrifying that it happens completely unprovoked. Am I fully alert? Yes. Yes, absolutely. I'm completely awake, my eyes are open, I'm fully conscious of my surroundings. It's not like the blank spells where I lose time and come back confused. When I hear the voices, I am wide awake and, as far as I can tell, thinking as clearly as I ever do these days. 

Like I was saying, it happens when the house is totally quiet, right? I'm just sitting there, maybe I have a cup of tea, I'm fully aware that I'm in my living room, I know what time it is, I know my husband is at work. I'm just trying to relax. And then, clear as day, just like you and I are talking right now, I hear them. Calling my name, saying I caused trouble on the block, saying the neighbors are angry. And because I'm so alert, my immediate reaction is to get up and check. I walk over to the window, I pull back the curtains, I look out at the street. I'm actively looking for the source of the sound because it's so real. If I were asleep or groggy, I wouldn't do that, you know? I'm fully processing what they're saying, which is why it hurts so much.

And it's the exact same thing when I'm out near the work zone. I'm standing there, gripping my sign, I'm watching the traffic, I'm doing my job. I know exactly where I am. I can feel the heat radiating off the asphalt, I can smell the diesel, I am completely grounded in reality. And then, boom. Over the sound of the milling machines and the dump trucks, there they are. They sound like they're right next to my ear. It just adds to this whole nightmare, you know? Between the blank spells and the heavy fog and now these voices... I just feel like my brain is completely betraying me. But no, to answer your question, no strange smells. I'm completely awake, my eyes are open, I'm fully conscious of my surroundings. It's not like the blank spells where I lose time and come back confused. I'm just sitting there, maybe I have a cup of tea, I'm fully aware that I'm in my living room, I know what time it is, I know my husband is at work. I'm just trying to relax. And then, clear as day, just like you and I are talking right now, I hear them. Calling my name, saying I caused trouble on the block, saying the neighbors are angry. And because I'm so alert, my immediate reaction is to get up and check. I walk over to the window, I pull back the curtains, I look out at the street. I'm actively looking for the source of the sound because it's so real. If I were asleep or groggy, I wouldn't do that, you know? I'm fully processing what they're saying, which is why it hurts so much.\n\nAnd it's the exact same thing when I'm out near the work zone. I'm standing there, gripping my sign, I'm watching the traffic, I'm doing my job. I know exactly where I am. I can feel the heat radiating off the asphalt, I can smell the diesel, I am completely grounded in reality. And then, boom. Over the sound of the milling machines and the dump trucks, there they are. Calling my name again, telling me I'm messing up the pattern, that I'm causing trouble. And again, because I'm fully alert, I react! I turn my head, I scan the crew, I look at Dave, I look at the guys on the pavers, trying to figure out who is yelling at me. I'm fully present, trying to solve the problem of who is speaking to me. \n\nSo, yes, I am completely awake and aware. Which honestly makes it so much more terrifying. If I were half-asleep or waking up from a dream, I could just brush it off as my brain playing tricks on me in a sleepy haze. But I'm not. I'm standing there, fully alert, and I'm the only one who hears them. Nobody else even flinches. It's just me, wide awake, listening to these awful things.\n\nDoctor: Did the voices start around the same time as the blank spells?\n\nPatient: Did they start around the same time? Well, let me really think about the timeline. I remember because it was right around the end of the summer paving season last year, just as we were moving into fall. The leaves were starting to turn, the mornings were getting that crisp chill, and we were doing this massive, weeks-long milling project out on Route 9. \n\nAnd honestly, it wasn't just the voices that started back then, either. That was right around the exact same time I started getting this overwhelming feeling... this really intense, undeniable sensation that things around me were communicating, or, well, sending messages specifically about me. No, I wouldn't say I get a headache. \n\nI mean, my head feels... full, I guess? But not in a painful way. It's more of that thick, heavy fog I was talking about earlier. It's like my brain is just exhausted from having to reboot itself. Sometimes my neck gets a little stiff, but I think that's just because I tense up so much when the panic sets in. You know, when I realize I've lost time again and I'm frantically looking around at the traffic and the construction equipment, my shoulders just migrate right up to my ears. I'm gripping that stop-slow paddle so tight my knuckles turn white. So any tension I feel up there is definitely just from the sheer stress of the situation, not an actual headache from the spell itself.\n\nIt's actually kind of surprising, now that I think about it. You'd think with how jarring it is to have your consciousness just blip out like that, your brain would hurt afterward. Like a computer overheating or something. But no, no throbbing, no sharp pains, no migraines. Just the confusion and the terror and that awful, sinking feeling that I'm losing my grip on things. \n\nI do get headaches sometimes, obviously, just from being out in the sun all day, the glare off the asphalt, the exhaust fumes from the diesel trucks... it's a harsh environment. But those are totally separate. They don't happen right after the blank spells. The blank spells just leave me feeling completely drained and terrified, but physically, my head doesn't hurt. It's just the mental toll that's so heavy.\n\nDoctor: Right before one of these blank spells starts, do you ever suddenly notice a strange smell that isn’t really there?\n\nPatient: A strange smell? Like, before the blank spells? Um, no. I haven't noticed any weird smells like burning rubber or toast or anything like that. I know people talk about smelling things before seizures or migraines, but no, my nose isn't picking up anything out of the ordinary. \n\nBut, you know, since you're asking about things that aren't really there... it's not smells, but it's sounds. I didn't even know how to bring this up, because it sounds so crazy, but... I hear things. It's not right before the blank spells, it's just... it happens. \n\nLike, I'll be at home, right? The house is completely quiet. My husband is at work, the TV is off, I'm just sitting on the couch trying to decompress from the day. And clear as day, I will hear these voices. It's not just a murmur, it's distinct. They call my name. \"Hey!\" or \"Look what she did.\" And they're always saying these awful things, telling me that I caused trouble on the block, that the neighbors are mad at me, that I did something wrong. And I'll get up and look out the window, and there's no one there. The street is empty. \n\nAnd it happens at work, too! I'll be standing near the work zone, and you know how loud it is out there—the milling machines, the dump trucks, the asphalt pavers, it's deafening. But somehow, over all that noise, I hear them again. Calling my name. Saying I'm messing up the traffic pattern, that I'm causing trouble for the crew. I'll spin around, thinking Dave or one of the other guys is yelling at me, but they're all focused on their jobs. Nobody else hears it. Just me. \n\nIt's so incredibly distressing. Because I know, logically, that nobody is standing in my quiet living room yelling at me, and I know that the guys on the crew wouldn't be saying those things, but the voices sound so real. They sound like they're right next to my ear. It just adds to this whole nightmare, you know? Between the blank spells and the heavy fog and now these voices... I just feel like my brain is completely betraying me. But no, to answer your question, no strange smells. Just... just the voices.\n\nDoctor: When you hear those voices, are you fully alert and thinking clearly at the time?\n\nPatient: Am I fully alert? Yes. Yes, absolutely. I'm completely awake, my eyes are open, I'm fully conscious of my surroundings. It's not like the blank spells where I lose time and come back confused. When I hear the voices, I am wide awake and, as far as I can tell, thinking as clearly as I ever do these days. \n\nLike I was saying, it happens when the house is totally quiet, right? I'm just sitting there, maybe I have a cup of tea, I'm fully aware that I'm in my living room, I know what time it is, I know my husband is at work. I'm just trying to relax. And then, clear as day, just like you and I are talking right now, I hear them. Calling my name, saying I caused trouble on the block, saying the neighbors are angry. And because I'm so alert, my immediate reaction is to get up and check. I walk over to the window, I pull back the curtains, I look out at the street. I'm actively looking for the source of the sound because it's so real. If I were asleep or groggy, I wouldn't do that, you know? I'm fully processing what they're saying, which is why it hurts so much.\n\nAnd it's the exact same thing when I'm out near the work zone. I'm standing there, gripping my sign, I'm watching the traffic, I'm doing my job. I know exactly where I am. I can feel the heat radiating off the asphalt, I can smell the diesel, I am completely grounded in reality. And then, boom. Over the sound of the milling machines and the dump trucks, there they are. Calling my name again, telling me I'm messing up the pattern, that I'm causing trouble. And again, because I'm fully alert, I react! I turn my head, I scan the crew, I look at Dave, I look at the guys on the pavers, trying to figure out who is yelling at me. I'm fully present, trying to solve the problem of who is speaking to me. \n\nSo, yes, I am completely awake and aware. Which honestly makes it so much more terrifying. If I were half-asleep or waking up from a dream, I could just brush it off as my brain playing tricks on me in a sleepy haze. But I'm not. I'm standing there, fully alert, and I'm the only one who hears them. Nobody else even flinches. It's just me, wide awake, listening to these awful things.\n\nDoctor: Did the voices start around the same time as the blank spells?\n\nPatient: Did they start around the same time? Well, let me really think about the timeline. Time gets so blurry for me lately with that heavy mental fog and the blank spells, but... if I really sit down and map it out, no, I don't think they started exactly at the same time. \n\nIf I'm being precise, the voices... they've been happening for about a year and four months now. I remember because it was right around the end of the summer paving season last year, just as we were moving into fall. The leaves were starting to turn, the mornings were getting that crisp chill, and we were doing this massive, weeks-long milling project out on Route 9. \n\nAnd honestly, it wasn't just the voices that started back then, either. That was right around the exact same time I started getting this overwhelming feeling... this really intense, undeniable sensation that things around me were communicating, or, well, sending messages specifically about me. Like the construction signs? You know those big electronic message boards we set up on the shoulder of the highway to warn drivers? I would look at them and feel completely certain that the flashing text was directed at me, like it was a hidden warning or a message about my life. \n\nAnd it was the trucks, too. The big dump trucks rolling past... the specific way they revved their engines or the pattern of their air brakes, it felt like a code that was entirely about me. Even the two-way radios the crew uses! I would hear the static and the chatter from the foreman's radio, and I just *knew*, deep down in my bones, that they were broadcasting things about me, sending these secret messages to everyone else on the site. \n\nSo, yeah, that whole nightmare—the voices calling my name, the radios, the trucks, the signs—that all started together about a year and four months ago. It's been such a incredibly long time to carry all of this. You have no idea how exhausting it is to put on a high-vis vest and go out to a work zone every single day for sixteen months, feeling like the actual machinery and the equipment are sending signals about you. And then you go home to a completely empty, quiet house, and the voices are waiting for you there, too. It's just been a year and four months of constant, relentless noise and messages, no matter where I am or what I'm doing.\n\nDoctor: When one of these blank spells ends, can you remember what happened during the spell itself?\n\nPatient: Remember what happened? No. No, not at all. It’s just... a complete void. And honestly, doctor, that is exactly why I finally came in to see you. Because my mind just keeps going completely, totally blank at the absolute worst possible times. \n\nLike, I’ll be out there on the site, right? And I will look down at the road-closure forms that we have to fill out for the city, or I'll literally just be standing there holding my stop-slow paddle... and suddenly, I cannot remember the steps I have done for years. I just can't remember what I'm supposed to be doing. I'm looking at this paddle, or looking at this standard paperwork, and I have done this exact routine every single day for years. Years! I have a bachelor's degree, I'm an educated person, I know how to manage a basic traffic pattern. But in those moments, it's like someone just pulls the plug on my brain. All the information just drains out.\n\nSo when the spell finally ends, and the fog kind of lifts and I snap back to reality, I don't remember a single thing that happened or how much time passed while I was out of it. All I know is that I'm suddenly standing there, staring at my equipment, trying desperately to piece together what I was just doing. And it is so incredibly terrifying, you know? Because you have impatient commuters in their cars flying by, and the paving crew is relying on me to keep them safe, and I'm just standing there with a totally blank mind, having to re-teach myself how to do a job I've done a thousand times before. It's just a total blackout of my thoughts, and then I'm left dealing with the panic of not knowing what just happened.\n\nDoctor: Have the voices been happening regularly for more than a month?\n\nPatient: More than a month? Oh, yes, absolutely. Like I was saying just a few minutes ago, it’s been a year and four months now. And when you ask if it’s regular... I mean, I honestly wish it was just a monthly thing, or even just a couple of times a week. That would be a vacation compared to this. But it is every single day. \n\nIt’s so regular it just completely wears you down to the bone. I'll be out there on the asphalt—Tuesday morning, Wednesday afternoon, Friday evening, it really doesn't matter what day of the week it is. I'm gripping that sign, trying to focus on the traffic pattern, and there they are. And you'd think maybe I'd get a weekend off, right? Like, maybe on a Sunday when I'm just sitting in my living room trying to drink my tea or fold a basket of laundry, they'd give me a break. But no. \n\nIt never stops. Every single day I wake up and I just know, I just absolutely know I'm going to hear them telling me I'm causing trouble or messing things up. It's just a relentless, everyday thing that I can't ever seem to get away from, no matter how hard I try to just focus on my job or my home.\n\nDoctor: Right before a blank spell starts, do you ever feel a sudden rising sensation in your stomach?\n\nPatient: A rising sensation in my stomach? My hands are still gripping the pole, my feet are still planted on the ground, usually right on the white line where I was standing before. Maybe I'm still slowly turning the sign or shifting my weight? I honestly have no idea. It's so frustrating not knowing what my own body is doing. It's not just a momentary lapse when I'm dozing off; it's happening at the absolute worst possible times. I'll be out there on the job, and I'll look down at the road-closure forms I need to fill out, or I'll be holding the stop-slow paddle, and suddenly... my mind just completely empties out. \n\nIt's terrifying, honestly. I've been doing this job for years. I know the procedures backwards and forwards. I know exactly how to set up the cone taper, I know the distance we need for the advance warning signs based on the speed limit. It's second nature to me. But then, right in the middle of a shift, with cars lining up and the paving crew waiting on my signal, I'll look at the paddle in my hand and I just... I cannot remember the steps. I can't remember what I'm supposed to do next. It's like someone just took an eraser to my brain for a few minutes. I'm standing there, supposed to be directing traffic and keeping everyone safe, and my mind is just a total, terrifying blank. So, no, it's not in bed. It's right out there in the middle of the road when I need my brain the most.\n\nDoctor: Right before one of the blank spells, do you ever suddenly feel a sense of déjà vu?\n\nPatient: Déjà vu? It's just... it's just this heavy, dark feeling. \n\nI mean, I stand on the same stretches of highway for hours, days, sometimes weeks at a time when we're doing a big milling and paving project. You'd think I'd have déjà vu all the time just because the job is so incredibly repetitive. You stand there, you flip the sign to \"Stop,\" you wait for the pilot car to come back around, you flip it to \"Slow.\" Over and over and over. \n\nBut right before my brain just shuts off? No, there's no sudden mystical feeling of \"Oh, I've lived this exact second before.\" It's more just... a total collapse of everything. The sadness just kind of pools up in me, this horrible, heavy emptiness, and then the fog rolls in and wipes the slate clean. It's not a memory playing tricks on me. It's just my mind giving up. I wish it was something as simple as déjà vu, honestly. People talk about déjà vu like it's this quirky, interesting little glitch in the matrix, you know? Like, \"Oh wow, how weird, I feel like I've had this conversation before.\" But what happens to me isn't quirky. It's devastating. It's like I cease to exist for a few minutes, right there on the hot asphalt, with cars whizzing past me. So, no, no déjà vu. Just the dread, and then the blankness."
